... The sound is 120 Hz, to be exact, and amps and volts are unimportant here, other than more amps make a louder sound, and more volts can create a longer, smoother sounding arc.

Power in the US is alternating current at 60 Hz, or cycles per second. In each cycle, the power moves in one direction, stops very briefly, then moves in the other direction, then stops very briefly again, before continuing on into the next cycle. So the power is actually turning on and off twice during each cycle, or 120 times per second. This switching happens smoothly, and if you were to connect a speaker directly to a low voltage AC power source, you would hear a nice pure sine-wave 60 Hz tone, because a speaker is designed to accurately convert the power waves in the wires into identical sound waves in the air. The speaker cone moves inward or outward from its center resting (off) position, in response to the direction of power flow.

However in the case of electrical arcs, each of the 'on' periods is actually creating separate 'bang' sound from the expanding air around the arc. So you get 2 bangs per cycle, or 120 bangs per second, which creates a distorted 120 Hz tone. As a matter of fact, most electric motors, transformers, buzzers, and such operating on 60 Hz power, actually create a 120 Hz tone for similar reasons, parts that move in the same direction, no matter which way the power is flowing.

In some other countries, power lines operate at 50 Hz, creating 100 Hz sounds. There are 50 Hz arcs here on YouTube. ﻿

In military and some other cases different Hz than 60 or 50Hz is used, so you can tell from sound what is going on.
